summary:
I built a web application that merges 25 years of MODIS and VIIRS active-fire records into one consistent burning-activity calendar for any area of interest. VIIRS (375 m) detects far more small fires than MODIS (1 km), so joining the two records makes it look as if fires jumped in 2012, when only the satellite changed.

PYROCHRON removes that artefact. It fills the gaps in the early Terra-only years and uses quantile mapping to convert VIIRS counts into MODIS-equivalent values. Users can then switch between as-reported, harmonized and anomaly views of a year-by-day calendar. The app highlights fire seasons, peak burning days, unusual weeks and long-term trends. Users can also upload their own NASA FIRMS data, and the analysis runs entirely in the browser.

This matters because emergency responders, scientists and land managers need records they can compare across years to anticipate critical fire periods, focus monitoring and respond earlier. PYROCHRON makes that possible anywhere in the world, from Andhra Pradesh to California, with free NASA data.
details:
PYROCHRON: The Harmonized Burn Calendar

What it does and how it works:

Since 2000, MODIS (1 km) and VIIRS (375 m) satellites have detected active fires. VIIRS sees smaller fires, so it counts several times more hotspots than MODIS. If you join the two records naively, it looks as if fires suddenly jumped in 2012, when only the sensor changed.

PYROCHRON harmonizes both records into one MODIS-equivalent burning-activity calendar for any area of interest. The method has four steps:

Align: daily hotspot counts per sensor, tracking when each sensor started (Terra 2000, Aqua 2002, VIIRS 2012).

Gap-fill: Terra-only years are scaled using the Terra share measured while Aqua overlaps.

Quantile-map: over the overlap period, VIIRS daily counts are mapped onto the MODIS distribution. This keeps rank order and handles nonlinearity and days with zero fires.

Anomaly detection: the series is smoothed over 7 days, put on a log scale, and compared with each day-of-year’s own climatology as a z-score.

The user sees a year-by-day calendar with three views: Harmonized, As-reported (which shows the fake 2012 jump) and Anomaly. The app also reports the fire season window, the peak burning day, the most extreme week, the worst year, and the trend before and after harmonization. Users can upload their own NASA FIRMS CSV files (MODIS and VIIRS together) and the whole analysis runs in their browser.

Benefits:

It gives one consistent 25-year record, so trends are not distorted by the change of satellite.

It shows fire managers when the season usually starts and ends, and when conditions are unusual.

It needs no installation, account or server. It runs in any browser, so it works in low-resource settings.

Anyone can reproduce the result with free NASA data.

Intended impact:

The aim is to help early-warning teams, emergency responders, scientists and land managers plan for fire seasons using a record that can be compared year to year. Locally, the same tool can be used for regions such as Rayalaseema in Andhra Pradesh, where dry-season crop-residue and scrub burning is common. It can also be used anywhere else in the world that FIRMS covers, so it connects communities in very different places.

Tools and technology:

HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with the HTML canvas for the visualizations. There are no frameworks or servers.

NASA FIRMS active-fire archive (MODIS and VIIRS S-NPP) as the intended real data source.

Hosted on GitHub Pages.

AI assistance (Claude by Anthropic) was used to help design and write the code and this description. (Check the Space Apps rules on disclosing AI use and state it accurately.)

No special hardware is needed.

Creativity:

The calendar format turns 25 years of fires into one picture: seasons appear as bands, and bad years stand out.

The As-reported to Harmonized toggle lets people see the sensor artefact disappear, which makes the idea easy to grasp.

The design uses an ember colour scale and is built to read like a “fire clock” of the planet.

It uses quantile mapping, a standard method from climate science, for a problem where a single scale factor would not work.

Factors I considered:

Different sensitivity: VIIRS detects more fires than MODIS because of its resolution, and the relationship is not a straight line. This is why we used quantile mapping instead of a simple multiplier.

Sensor timeline: Terra-only years undercount compared with Terra plus Aqua.

Double counting: we use only VIIRS S-NPP. NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 would count the same fires again and bring back the artificial jump.

Same area for both sensors, so the comparison is fair.

Honesty about the data: the preset regions in the demo use simulated data that mimics sensor behaviour. Real analysis uses uploaded FIRMS data.

Limits: hotspot counts are not burned area or fire size, and clouds and the overpass time affect detection. FRP weighting and confidence filtering are future work.

Accessibility: it runs in the browser, so no data leaves the user’s computer.
